Regarding the Southern and Northern Dynasties period, the {{ill|History of the Southern Dynasties|ja|南史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Song Dynasty (Southern)|ja|宋 (南朝)|lt=Southern Song|lt_ja=宋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records in Volume 2 that the deposed former emperor {{ill|Former Deposed Emperor|ja|前廃帝 (南朝宋)|lt=Former Deposed Emperor|lt_ja=前廃帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the {{ill|Princess of the Mountain Shade|ja|山陰公主|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and several hundred {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, followed an assembly of shamans to capture ghosts; further mentions of Uneme appear in Volume 11 in the biography of {{ill|Chen Miaodeng|ja|陳妙登|lt=Later Deposed Empress Chen|lt_ja=後廃帝陳太妃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" /> In the {{ill|Book of Northern History|ja|北史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Northern Wei|ja|北魏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (or later Wei), Volume 13 of the consorts’ records notes the existence of the Uneme system, and Volume 10 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou|ja|宣帝 (北周)|lt=Emperor Xuan|lt_ja=宣帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes an account of Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" />
During the {{ill|Sui Dynasty|ja|隋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} period, Volume 675 of the {{ill|Wenyuan Yinghua|ja|文苑英華|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that in Emperor {{ill|Yang of Sui|ja|煬帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s harem there were said to be several hundred to a thousand Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to {{ill|Zhao Yi|ja|趙翼|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Uneme also existed during the era of the {{ill|Yuan Dynasty|ja|元 (王朝)|lt=Yuan|lt_ja=元|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as recorded in Volume 30 of the {{ill|Annotated Twenty-Two Histories|ja|二十二史箚記|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in Japan == The earliest mention of Uneme appears in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe">{{Cite journal |type=Japanese book |url=https://doi.org/10.5955/jalha.1951.96 |author={{ill|Sogabe Shizuo|ja|曽我部静雄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=The Origins of Attendants, Uneme, and Female Servants |journal=Studies in Legal History |issue=1 |publisher=Legal History Society |date=1951 |pages=96–119}}</ref>
In the 2nd year of the {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (807 AD), the system of Uneme offerings was temporarily abolished, but it was revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, the position was reserved only for special ceremonies. The head official of the Uneme was known as Uneme-no-Kami.
=== History === Although many aspects of its origins remain unclear, according to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as early as the {{ill|Asuka Period|ja|飛鳥時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, local aristocrats customarily offered their daughters to the {{ill|Imperial Household|ja|皇室|lt=Imperial Family|lt_ja=天皇家|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Successive generations of Uneme were drawn from the direct families of the emperor as well as from prominent local clans. Moreover, a Taihōkan edict issued in the 17th year of the {{ill|Engi|ja|延喜|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (917 AD, as indicated by {{ill|917|ja|917|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) by which the governor of Izumo Province (<now rendered as> {{ill|Izumo Provincial Governor|ja|出雲国造|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) prohibited keeping a concubine under the title {{ill|Jingu Uneme|ja|神宮采女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, except in cases necessary for Shinto ritual, has been cited as evidence that the system emerged during the process in which the imperial family gradually absorbed and integrated local ritual functions. Some scholars have even suggested that Uneme, who were sometimes treated as equivalent to concubines in ritual practices that sometimes involved procreation, may have had their origins in associations with {{ill|Shrine Maidens|ja|巫女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>『古代豪族』, Aoki Kazuo</ref>
Although their principal duty was to serve in the meal preparations for the emperor, Uneme – who were exclusively selected from among those admired for their beauty from all over the country and who served in close proximity to the emperor – often also fulfilled the role of concubines and bore children. However, as social status at that time placed great importance on the mother’s family background, children born to Uneme from local aristocratic families (the families of {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and above) were generally accorded a lower status compared with those born to central aristocrats or the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The system was formalized by the Imperial Harem Officials Order of the {{ill|Taibō Ritsuryō|ja|大宝律令|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Its provisions were as follows: : An edict issued by the {{ill|Ministry of Central Affairs|ja|中務省|1=Ministry of the Center|qq=draft|qq=draft}} allocated quotas to the provinces for recruitment, though the process was nominally termed an “offering.” : The eligibility criteria were: # The candidate had to be between 13 and 30 years old. (In the revived system during {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s reign – after the temporary abolition of the offering system – the age requirement was 16 to 20.) # The candidate had to be a daughter or sister of a family of at least {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} Rank. # Their appearance had to be especially refined. : Although the personnel matters of these women were managed by the “Uneme Department” ({{ill|Uneme Department|ja|采女司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) under the {{ill|Imperial Household Ministry|ja|宮内省 (律令制)|lt=Imperial Household Ministry|lt_ja=宮内省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in practice they were assigned to two of the Twelve Harem Departments: 6 to the {{ill|Water Department|ja|水司|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 60 to the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Although the official quota was 66, the military defense provisions of the Taibō Ritsuryō stipulated that Uneme should be recruited from one-third of the provinces nationwide; thus, the actual number of Uneme offered greatly exceeded the official quota. It is therefore believed that there were also individuals placed in other departments as substitutes for {{ill|Onamutsu|ja|女嬬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or who were employed outside the official quota,<ref>『郡司及び采女制度の研究』, Isokai Masayoshi</ref> or even those attached to imperial princes,<ref>『奈良の都』, Aoki Kazuo</ref> and that some, such as {{ill|Iitakushotaka|ja|飯高諸高|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were later promoted to higher positions (such as {{ill|Dianshi|ja|典侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Chief Attendant|ja|掌侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Head of the Serving Department|ja|掌膳|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Official Sweeper|ja|典掃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), which were also considered outside the official Uneme quota. In this period when Uneme were integrated into the {{ill|Ritsuryō System|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, their role as wives or concubines of the emperor diminished, and they increasingly came to be regarded as lower-Ranking officials within the imperial harem. Many of them likely became {{ill|Maid|ja|女孺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite book |author={{ill|Keiji Nagahara|ja|永原慶二|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=Iwanami Dictionary of Japanese History |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |date=1999}}</ref>
Reforms under {{ill|Emperor Heizei|ja|平城天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} abolished the system of Uneme offerings, and accordingly the Uneme Department was also dissolved, being merged with the Department of Sewing ({{ill|Department of Sewing|ja|縫部司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in the {{ill|Sewing Hall|ja|縫殿寮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Ministry of Finance|ja|大蔵省 (律令制)|1=Ministry of the Treasury|lt=Finance Ministry|lt_ja=大蔵省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. However, the offering system and the Uneme Department were revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|Engishiki|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the official quota for Uneme was reduced to 41 in the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 6 in the {{ill|Cleaning Department|ja|掃司|lt=Kanomori no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かにもりのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, Uneme were increasingly selected from the daughters of central nobles, and the role became increasingly ceremonial. From the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} onward, Uneme were chosen from among the court ladies only at the time of the {{ill|Enthronement Ceremony|ja|即位の礼|lt=Enthronement Ceremony|lt_ja=即位式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} for the emperor; at that time, instead of wearing the full formal attire of the court ladies ({{ill|Junihitoe|ja|十二単|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), they donned a special, short {{ill|Uneme Costume|ja|采女装束|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Etymology === Several theories have been proposed regarding the origin of the word “uneme.” These include {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|ja|本居宣長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unagee” theory (嬰部（うなげえ）), {{ill|Ogyū Sorai|ja|荻生徂徠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unawime” theory (項意（うなゐめ）), {{ill|Kamo no Maifuchi|ja|賀茂真淵|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unome” theory (氏之女（うのめ）), and {{ill|Tsuboi Yoshitomo|ja|壺井義知|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Uneme” theory (畝女（うねめ）).
=== Uneme as Objects of Admiration === Uneme were reputed to be largely drawn from local aristocratic families, celebrated for their exquisite beauty and high cultural accomplishments. Owing to the fact that only the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was permitted personal contact with them, they have long been objects of male admiration. In earlier times, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} describes the Uneme as having “exceptionally beautiful features and a refined appearance,” while the {{ill|Hyakuryō Kun'yōshū|ja|百寮訓要集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} states that “the Uneme are women selected from among the most beautiful in the land to serve the Son of Heaven.” The {{ill|Kokinshū|ja|古今集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also contains many gentle allusions in its poetry, and the {{ill|Wakan Kanjō Hisho|ja|和漢官職秘抄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that “in some accounts, either through the fame of a beauty or the renown of her poetry – or by virtue of a refined aptitude in playing the koto and the se – a woman would be presented by local officials.” Furthermore, the {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes the famous poem celebrating how {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|ja|藤原鎌足|qq=draft|qq=draft}} rejoiced at receiving the Uneme Yasumi from {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: “われはもや安見児得たり 皆人の得難にすとふ安見児得たり” In addition, a poem by {{ill|Prince Shiki|ja|志貴皇子|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—“The Uneme’s sleeves flutter, like the Asuka breeze, playfully blowing far from the capital”—reveals the deep admiration that men felt for these beautiful Uneme.
== Legendary Uneme == === The Legend of Sarusawa Pond / Yama no I Legend === : In the {{ill|Yamato Monogatari|ja|大和物語|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, there is a legend concerning the “Emperor of Nara” (displayed as {{ill|Tachibana Morone|ja|橘諸兄|lt=Katsuragi-ō|lt_ja=葛城王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and an Uneme known as Haruhime. : It is noteworthy that interpretations of the related Man'yōshū poems differ between the two versions—for instance, whether the poem “Even the shadows of Mount Azumi can be seen in the shallow heart of the mountain well” conveys a sentiment of passionate love or sincere devotion, and whether the poem “My sister’s disheveled hair, I see it sorrowfully in the jeweled waters of Sarusawa Pond” evokes the image of hair floating like seaweed from a drowned body or recalls the hair as it was in life. : On the basis of this legend, {{ill|Nara City|ja|奈良市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Koriyama City|ja|郡山市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} have established a sister cities relationship. * Sarusawa Pond *: According to both the account in the Yamato Monogatari and local tradition in Nara City, a certain Uneme—who had fallen out of favor with the “Emperor of Nara” (during the {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, referred to as Saru Tennō)—committed suicide by leaping into Sarusawa Pond. This event served as the motif for the {{ill|Uneme (Noh)|ja|采女 (謡曲)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. : As a memorial to her spirit, an annual festival – the {{ill|Uneme Festival|ja|采女祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – is held during the time of the {{ill|Mid-Autumn Moon|ja|中秋の名月|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at the {{ill|Uneme Shrine|ja|采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, located along the banks of {{ill|Sarusawa Pond|ja|猿沢池|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nara. * The Yama no I Legend *: In a legend from Koriyama City, a prelude and sequel exist: It is said that when the Katsuragi-ō (who had come on an inspection tour to Mutsu Province) first laid eyes on Haruhime, the daughter of the head of the Azumi village, he brought her back to the capital. However, missing her betrothed, Haruhime feigned an accidental plunge into Sarusawa Pond in order to return home. Later, after her lover cast himself into the clear waters of a mountain well, Haruhime followed him in a final act of suicide. In connection with this legend, the local {{ill|Uneme Shrine (Koriyama)|ja|采女神社 (郡山市)|lt=Uneme Shrine|lt_ja=采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} exists, as does a local festival – the {{ill|Koriyama Uneme Festival|ja|郡山うねめまつり|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – established at the time of the merger of Koriyama City and {{ill|Azumi District|ja|安積郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. There is also a tourism ambassador known as “Miss Uneme” who is selected through a {{ill|Miss Contest|ja|ミスコンテスト|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. === Kojiki Legend === : During the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} that “the threefold Uneme of {{ill|Ise Province|ja|伊勢の国|qq=draft|qq=draft}},” while serving at a banquet for the emperor, unwittingly poured wine into a ceremonial cup containing leaves. This act incurred the emperor’s wrath and nearly led to her execution; however, she spontaneously composed a poem extolling the emperor and praying for prosperity, and the excellence of her verse so impressed the emperor that her life was spared. Furthermore, a place named “Uneme” exists in both {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yokkaichi City|ja|四日市市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

'''Uneme''' (采女)
# In China, the term Uneme has two distinct meanings: # In China, Uneme (pronounced “saijo”) refers to an official system found in dynasties following the {{ill|Former Han Dynasty|ja|前漢|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, although it is not seen in the {{ill|Tang Dynasty|ja|唐|qq=draft|qq=draft}} system.<ref name="sogabe" /> # In Japan, Uneme (pronounced “uneme”) were court ladies who served in the {{ill|Imperial Court|ja|朝廷|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, attending closely to the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Empress|ja|皇后|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by managing meals and other daily affairs – an official post which existed until the early {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in China == === Han Dynasty === In the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, accounts are found in Volume 8 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Ling|ja|霊帝 (漢)|lt=Emperor Ling|lt_ja=霊帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and in Volume 10, Part 1 of the harem annals.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to the biography of {{ill|Lu Qiang|ja|呂強|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the number of harem {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was said to number in the thousands, with the term “Uneme” being synonymous with “Cai Nu”.<ref name="sogabe" /> Although the Uneme system was not adopted under the Tang system and was regarded as a Later Han institution, the first volume of the {{ill|Miscellaneous Records of Xijing|ja|西京雑記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} contains an account of “Cai Nu”, suggesting that its origins may extend as far back as the Former Han.<ref name="sogabe" />
=== After the Han Dynasty === The {{ill|Book of Jin|ja|晋書|qq=draft|qq=draft}} discusses the Uneme of {{ill|Emperor Wu of Jin|ja|司馬炎|lt=Emperor Wu of Jin|lt_ja=武帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, with accounts appearing in Volume 3 of the annals of Emperor Wu, Volume 57 of the biography of {{ill|Hu Fen|ja|胡奮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Volume 27 of the upper Five Elements Records, Volume 28 of the middle Five Elements Records, and Volume 31 of the consorts’ records.<ref name="sogabe" />

During the {{ill|Sui Dynasty|ja|隋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} period, Volume 675 of the {{ill|Wenyuan Yinghua|ja|文苑英華|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that in Emperor {{ill|Yang of Sui|ja|煬帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s harem there were said to be several hundred to a thousand Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to {{ill|Zhao Yi|ja|趙翼|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Uneme also existed during the era of the {{ill|Yuan Dynasty|ja|元 (王朝)|lt=Yuan|lt_ja=元|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as recorded in Volume 30 of the {{ill|Annotated Twenty-Two Histories|ja|二十二史箚記|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />

In the 2nd year of the {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (807 AD), the system of Uneme offerings was temporarily abolished, but it was revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, the position was reserved only for special ceremonies. The head official of the Uneme was known as Uneme-no-Kami.
=== History === Although many aspects of its origins remain unclear, according to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as early as the {{ill|Asuka Period|ja|飛鳥時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, local aristocrats customarily offered their daughters to the {{ill|Imperial Household|ja|皇室|lt=Imperial Family|lt_ja=天皇家|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Successive generations of Uneme were drawn from the direct families of the emperor as well as from prominent local clans. Moreover, a Taihōkan edict issued in the 17th year of the {{ill|Engi|ja|延喜|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (917 AD, as indicated by {{ill|917|ja|917|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) by which the governor of Izumo Province (<now rendered as> {{ill|Izumo Provincial Governor|ja|出雲国造|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) prohibited keeping a concubine under the title {{ill|Jingu Uneme|ja|神宮采女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, except in cases necessary for Shinto ritual, has been cited as evidence that the system emerged during the process in which the imperial family gradually absorbed and integrated local ritual functions. Some scholars have even suggested that Uneme, who were sometimes treated as equivalent to concubines in ritual practices that sometimes involved procreation, may have had their origins in associations with {{ill|Shrine Maidens|ja|巫女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>『古代豪族』, Aoki Kazuo</ref>
Although their principal duty was to serve in the meal preparations for the emperor, Uneme – who were exclusively selected from among those admired for their beauty from all over the country and who served in close proximity to the emperor – often also fulfilled the role of concubines and bore children. However, as social status at that time placed great importance on the mother’s family background, children born to Uneme from local aristocratic families (the families of {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and above) were generally accorded a lower status compared with those born to central aristocrats or the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The system was formalized by the Imperial Harem Officials Order of the {{ill|Taibō Ritsuryō|ja|大宝律令|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Its provisions were as follows: : An edict issued by the {{ill|Ministry of Central Affairs|ja|中務省|1=Ministry of the Center|qq=draft|qq=draft}} allocated quotas to the provinces for recruitment, though the process was nominally termed an “offering.” : The eligibility criteria were: # The candidate had to be between 13 and 30 years old. (In the revived system during {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s reign – after the temporary abolition of the offering system – the age requirement was 16 to 20.) # The candidate had to be a daughter or sister of a family of at least {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} Rank. # Their appearance had to be especially refined. : Although the personnel matters of these women were managed by the “Uneme Department” ({{ill|Uneme Department|ja|采女司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) under the {{ill|Imperial Household Ministry|ja|宮内省 (律令制)|lt=Imperial Household Ministry|lt_ja=宮内省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in practice they were assigned to two of the Twelve Harem Departments: 6 to the {{ill|Water Department|ja|水司|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 60 to the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Although the official quota was 66, the military defense provisions of the Taibō Ritsuryō stipulated that Uneme should be recruited from one-third of the provinces nationwide; thus, the actual number of Uneme offered greatly exceeded the official quota. It is therefore believed that there were also individuals placed in other departments as substitutes for {{ill|Onamutsu|ja|女嬬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or who were employed outside the official quota,<ref>『郡司及び采女制度の研究』, Isokai Masayoshi</ref> or even those attached to imperial princes,<ref>『奈良の都』, Aoki Kazuo</ref> and that some, such as {{ill|Iitakushotaka|ja|飯高諸高|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were later promoted to higher positions (such as {{ill|Dianshi|ja|典侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Chief Attendant|ja|掌侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Head of the Serving Department|ja|掌膳|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Official Sweeper|ja|典掃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), which were also considered outside the official Uneme quota. In this period when Uneme were integrated into the {{ill|Ritsuryō System|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, their role as wives or concubines of the emperor diminished, and they increasingly came to be regarded as lower-Ranking officials within the imperial harem. Many of them likely became {{ill|Maid|ja|女孺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite book |author={{ill|Keiji Nagahara|ja|永原慶二|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=Iwanami Dictionary of Japanese History |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |date=1999}}</ref>
Reforms under {{ill|Emperor Heizei|ja|平城天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} abolished the system of Uneme offerings, and accordingly the Uneme Department was also dissolved, being merged with the Department of Sewing ({{ill|Department of Sewing|ja|縫部司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in the {{ill|Sewing Hall|ja|縫殿寮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Ministry of Finance|ja|大蔵省 (律令制)|1=Ministry of the Treasury|lt=Finance Ministry|lt_ja=大蔵省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. However, the offering system and the Uneme Department were revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|Engishiki|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the official quota for Uneme was reduced to 41 in the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 6 in the {{ill|Cleaning Department|ja|掃司|lt=Kanomori no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かにもりのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, Uneme were increasingly selected from the daughters of central nobles, and the role became increasingly ceremonial. From the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} onward, Uneme were chosen from among the court ladies only at the time of the {{ill|Enthronement Ceremony|ja|即位の礼|lt=Enthronement Ceremony|lt_ja=即位式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} for the emperor; at that time, instead of wearing the full formal attire of the court ladies ({{ill|Junihitoe|ja|十二単|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), they donned a special, short {{ill|Uneme Costume|ja|采女装束|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Etymology === Several theories have been proposed regarding the origin of the word “uneme.” These include {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|ja|本居宣長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unagee” theory (嬰部（うなげえ）), {{ill|Ogyū Sorai|ja|荻生徂徠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unawime” theory (項意（うなゐめ）), {{ill|Kamo no Maifuchi|ja|賀茂真淵|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unome” theory (氏之女（うのめ）), and {{ill|Tsuboi Yoshitomo|ja|壺井義知|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Uneme” theory (畝女（うねめ）).
=== Uneme as Objects of Admiration === Uneme were reputed to be largely drawn from local aristocratic families, celebrated for their exquisite beauty and high cultural accomplishments. Owing to the fact that only the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was permitted personal contact with them, they have long been objects of male admiration. In earlier times, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} describes the Uneme as having “exceptionally beautiful features and a refined appearance,” while the {{ill|Hyakuryō Kun'yōshū|ja|百寮訓要集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} states that “the Uneme are women selected from among the most beautiful in the land to serve the Son of Heaven.” The {{ill|Kokinshū|ja|古今集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also contains many gentle allusions in its poetry, and the {{ill|Wakan Kanjō Hisho|ja|和漢官職秘抄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that “in some accounts, either through the fame of a beauty or the renown of her poetry – or by virtue of a refined aptitude in playing the koto and the se – a woman would be presented by local officials.” Furthermore, the {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes the famous poem celebrating how {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|ja|藤原鎌足|qq=draft|qq=draft}} rejoiced at receiving the Uneme Yasumi from {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: “われはもや安見児得たり 皆人の得難にすとふ安見児得たり” In addition, a poem by {{ill|Prince Shiki|ja|志貴皇子|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—“The Uneme’s sleeves flutter, like the Asuka breeze, playfully blowing far from the capital”—reveals the deep admiration that men felt for these beautiful Uneme.
== Legendary Uneme == === The Legend of Sarusawa Pond / Yama no I Legend === : In the {{ill|Yamato Monogatari|ja|大和物語|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, there is a legend concerning the “Emperor of Nara” (displayed as {{ill|Tachibana Morone|ja|橘諸兄|lt=Katsuragi-ō|lt_ja=葛城王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and an Uneme known as Haruhime. : It is noteworthy that interpretations of the related Man'yōshū poems differ between the two versions—for instance, whether the poem “Even the shadows of Mount Azumi can be seen in the shallow heart of the mountain well” conveys a sentiment of passionate love or sincere devotion, and whether the poem “My sister’s disheveled hair, I see it sorrowfully in the jeweled waters of Sarusawa Pond” evokes the image of hair floating like seaweed from a drowned body or recalls the hair as it was in life. : On the basis of this legend, {{ill|Nara City|ja|奈良市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Koriyama City|ja|郡山市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} have established a sister cities relationship. * Sarusawa Pond *: According to both the account in the Yamato Monogatari and local tradition in Nara City, a certain Uneme—who had fallen out of favor with the “Emperor of Nara” (during the {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, referred to as Saru Tennō)—committed suicide by leaping into Sarusawa Pond. This event served as the motif for the {{ill|Uneme (Noh)|ja|采女 (謡曲)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. : As a memorial to her spirit, an annual festival – the {{ill|Uneme Festival|ja|采女祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – is held during the time of the {{ill|Mid-Autumn Moon|ja|中秋の名月|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at the {{ill|Uneme Shrine|ja|采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, located along the banks of {{ill|Sarusawa Pond|ja|猿沢池|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nara. * The Yama no I Legend *: In a legend from Koriyama City, a prelude and sequel exist: It is said that when the Katsuragi-ō (who had come on an inspection tour to Mutsu Province) first laid eyes on Haruhime, the daughter of the head of the Azumi village, he brought her back to the capital. However, missing her betrothed, Haruhime feigned an accidental plunge into Sarusawa Pond in order to return home. Later, after her lover cast himself into the clear waters of a mountain well, Haruhime followed him in a final act of suicide. In connection with this legend, the local {{ill|Uneme Shrine (Koriyama)|ja|采女神社 (郡山市)|lt=Uneme Shrine|lt_ja=采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} exists, as does a local festival – the {{ill|Koriyama Uneme Festival|ja|郡山うねめまつり|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – established at the time of the merger of Koriyama City and {{ill|Azumi District|ja|安積郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. There is also a tourism ambassador known as “Miss Uneme” who is selected through a {{ill|Miss Contest|ja|ミスコンテスト|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. === Kojiki Legend === : During the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} that “the threefold Uneme of {{ill|Ise Province|ja|伊勢の国|qq=draft|qq=draft}},” while serving at a banquet for the emperor, unwittingly poured wine into a ceremonial cup containing leaves. This act incurred the emperor’s wrath and nearly led to her execution; however, she spontaneously composed a poem extolling the emperor and praying for prosperity, and the excellence of her verse so impressed the emperor that her life was spared. Furthermore, a place named “Uneme” exists in both {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yokkaichi City|ja|四日市市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

{{ill|Imperial Harem|ja|後宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Court Lady|ja|女官|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Former Han Dynasty|ja|前漢|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Tang Dynasty|ja|唐|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Imperial Court|ja|朝廷|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Empress|ja|皇后|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Official Position|ja|官職|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
'''Uneme''' (采女)
# In China, the term Uneme has two distinct meanings: # In China, Uneme (pronounced “saijo”) refers to an official system found in dynasties following the {{ill|Former Han Dynasty|ja|前漢|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, although it is not seen in the {{ill|Tang Dynasty|ja|唐|qq=draft|qq=draft}} system.<ref name="sogabe" /> # In Japan, Uneme (pronounced “uneme”) were court ladies who served in the {{ill|Imperial Court|ja|朝廷|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, attending closely to the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Empress|ja|皇后|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by managing meals and other daily affairs – an official post which existed until the early {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in China == === Han Dynasty === In the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, accounts are found in Volume 8 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Ling|ja|霊帝 (漢)|lt=Emperor Ling|lt_ja=霊帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and in Volume 10, Part 1 of the harem annals.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to the biography of {{ill|Lu Qiang|ja|呂強|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the number of harem {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was said to number in the thousands, with the term “Uneme” being synonymous with “Cai Nu”.<ref name="sogabe" /> Although the Uneme system was not adopted under the Tang system and was regarded as a Later Han institution, the first volume of the {{ill|Miscellaneous Records of Xijing|ja|西京雑記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} contains an account of “Cai Nu”, suggesting that its origins may extend as far back as the Former Han.<ref name="sogabe" />
=== After the Han Dynasty === The {{ill|Book of Jin|ja|晋書|qq=draft|qq=draft}} discusses the Uneme of {{ill|Emperor Wu of Jin|ja|司馬炎|lt=Emperor Wu of Jin|lt_ja=武帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, with accounts appearing in Volume 3 of the annals of Emperor Wu, Volume 57 of the biography of {{ill|Hu Fen|ja|胡奮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Volume 27 of the upper Five Elements Records, Volume 28 of the middle Five Elements Records, and Volume 31 of the consorts’ records.<ref name="sogabe" />
Regarding the Southern and Northern Dynasties period, the {{ill|History of the Southern Dynasties|ja|南史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Song Dynasty (Southern)|ja|宋 (南朝)|lt=Southern Song|lt_ja=宋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records in Volume 2 that the deposed former emperor {{ill|Former Deposed Emperor|ja|前廃帝 (南朝宋)|lt=Former Deposed Emperor|lt_ja=前廃帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the {{ill|Princess of the Mountain Shade|ja|山陰公主|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and several hundred {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, followed an assembly of shamans to capture ghosts; further mentions of Uneme appear in Volume 11 in the biography of {{ill|Chen Miaodeng|ja|陳妙登|lt=Later Deposed Empress Chen|lt_ja=後廃帝陳太妃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" /> In the {{ill|Book of Northern History|ja|北史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Northern Wei|ja|北魏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (or later Wei), Volume 13 of the consorts’ records notes the existence of the Uneme system, and Volume 10 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou|ja|宣帝 (北周)|lt=Emperor Xuan|lt_ja=宣帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes an account of Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" />
During the {{ill|Sui Dynasty|ja|隋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} period, Volume 675 of the {{ill|Wenyuan Yinghua|ja|文苑英華|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that in Emperor {{ill|Yang of Sui|ja|煬帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s harem there were said to be several hundred to a thousand Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to {{ill|Zhao Yi|ja|趙翼|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Uneme also existed during the era of the {{ill|Yuan Dynasty|ja|元 (王朝)|lt=Yuan|lt_ja=元|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as recorded in Volume 30 of the {{ill|Annotated Twenty-Two Histories|ja|二十二史箚記|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in Japan == The earliest mention of Uneme appears in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe">{{Cite journal |type=Japanese book |url=https://doi.org/10.5955/jalha.1951.96 |author={{ill|Sogabe Shizuo|ja|曽我部静雄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=The Origins of Attendants, Uneme, and Female Servants |journal=Studies in Legal History |issue=1 |publisher=Legal History Society |date=1951 |pages=96–119}}</ref>
In the 2nd year of the {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (807 AD), the system of Uneme offerings was temporarily abolished, but it was revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, the position was reserved only for special ceremonies. The head official of the Uneme was known as Uneme-no-Kami.

(In the revived system during {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s reign – after the temporary abolition of the offering system – the age requirement was 16 to 20.) # The candidate had to be a daughter or sister of a family of at least {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} Rank. # Their appearance had to be especially refined. : Although the personnel matters of these women were managed by the “Uneme Department” ({{ill|Uneme Department|ja|采女司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) under the {{ill|Imperial Household Ministry|ja|宮内省 (律令制)|lt=Imperial Household Ministry|lt_ja=宮内省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in practice they were assigned to two of the Twelve Harem Departments: 6 to the {{ill|Water Department|ja|水司|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 60 to the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Although the official quota was 66, the military defense provisions of the Taibō Ritsuryō stipulated that Uneme should be recruited from one-third of the provinces nationwide; thus, the actual number of Uneme offered greatly exceeded the official quota. It is therefore believed that there were also individuals placed in other departments as substitutes for {{ill|Onamutsu|ja|女嬬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or who were employed outside the official quota,<ref>『郡司及び采女制度の研究』, Isokai Masayoshi</ref> or even those attached to imperial princes,<ref>『奈良の都』, Aoki Kazuo</ref> and that some, such as {{ill|Iitakushotaka|ja|飯高諸高|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were later promoted to higher positions (such as {{ill|Dianshi|ja|典侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Chief Attendant|ja|掌侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Head of the Serving Department|ja|掌膳|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Official Sweeper|ja|典掃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), which were also considered outside the official Uneme quota. In this period when Uneme were integrated into the {{ill|Ritsuryō System|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, their role as wives or concubines of the emperor diminished, and they increasingly came to be regarded as lower-Ranking officials within the imperial harem. Many of them likely became {{ill|Maid|ja|女孺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite book |author={{ill|Keiji Nagahara|ja|永原慶二|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=Iwanami Dictionary of Japanese History |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |date=1999}}</ref>
Reforms under {{ill|Emperor Heizei|ja|平城天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} abolished the system of Uneme offerings, and accordingly the Uneme Department was also dissolved, being merged with the Department of Sewing ({{ill|Department of Sewing|ja|縫部司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in the {{ill|Sewing Hall|ja|縫殿寮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Ministry of Finance|ja|大蔵省 (律令制)|1=Ministry of the Treasury|lt=Finance Ministry|lt_ja=大蔵省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. However, the offering system and the Uneme Department were revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|Engishiki|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the official quota for Uneme was reduced to 41 in the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 6 in the {{ill|Cleaning Department|ja|掃司|lt=Kanomori no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かにもりのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, Uneme were increasingly selected from the daughters of central nobles, and the role became increasingly ceremonial. From the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} onward, Uneme were chosen from among the court ladies only at the time of the {{ill|Enthronement Ceremony|ja|即位の礼|lt=Enthronement Ceremony|lt_ja=即位式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} for the emperor; at that time, instead of wearing the full formal attire of the court ladies ({{ill|Junihitoe|ja|十二単|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), they donned a special, short {{ill|Uneme Costume|ja|采女装束|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Etymology === Several theories have been proposed regarding the origin of the word “uneme.” These include {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|ja|本居宣長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unagee” theory (嬰部（うなげえ）), {{ill|Ogyū Sorai|ja|荻生徂徠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unawime” theory (項意（うなゐめ）), {{ill|Kamo no Maifuchi|ja|賀茂真淵|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unome” theory (氏之女（うのめ）), and {{ill|Tsuboi Yoshitomo|ja|壺井義知|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Uneme” theory (畝女（うねめ）).
=== Uneme as Objects of Admiration === Uneme were reputed to be largely drawn from local aristocratic families, celebrated for their exquisite beauty and high cultural accomplishments. Owing to the fact that only the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was permitted personal contact with them, they have long been objects of male admiration. In earlier times, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} describes the Uneme as having “exceptionally beautiful features and a refined appearance,” while the {{ill|Hyakuryō Kun'yōshū|ja|百寮訓要集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} states that “the Uneme are women selected from among the most beautiful in the land to serve the Son of Heaven.” The {{ill|Kokinshū|ja|古今集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also contains many gentle allusions in its poetry, and the {{ill|Wakan Kanjō Hisho|ja|和漢官職秘抄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that “in some accounts, either through the fame of a beauty or the renown of her poetry – or by virtue of a refined aptitude in playing the koto and the se – a woman would be presented by local officials.” Furthermore, the {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes the famous poem celebrating how {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|ja|藤原鎌足|qq=draft|qq=draft}} rejoiced at receiving the Uneme Yasumi from {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: “われはもや安見児得たり 皆人の得難にすとふ安見児得たり” In addition, a poem by {{ill|Prince Shiki|ja|志貴皇子|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—“The Uneme’s sleeves flutter, like the Asuka breeze, playfully blowing far from the capital”—reveals the deep admiration that men felt for these beautiful Uneme.
== Legendary Uneme == === The Legend of Sarusawa Pond / Yama no I Legend === : In the {{ill|Yamato Monogatari|ja|大和物語|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, there is a legend concerning the “Emperor of Nara” (displayed as {{ill|Tachibana Morone|ja|橘諸兄|lt=Katsuragi-ō|lt_ja=葛城王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and an Uneme known as Haruhime. : It is noteworthy that interpretations of the related Man'yōshū poems differ between the two versions—for instance, whether the poem “Even the shadows of Mount Azumi can be seen in the shallow heart of the mountain well” conveys a sentiment of passionate love or sincere devotion, and whether the poem “My sister’s disheveled hair, I see it sorrowfully in the jeweled waters of Sarusawa Pond” evokes the image of hair floating like seaweed from a drowned body or recalls the hair as it was in life. : On the basis of this legend, {{ill|Nara City|ja|奈良市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Koriyama City|ja|郡山市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} have established a sister cities relationship. * Sarusawa Pond *: According to both the account in the Yamato Monogatari and local tradition in Nara City, a certain Uneme—who had fallen out of favor with the “Emperor of Nara” (during the {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, referred to as Saru Tennō)—committed suicide by leaping into Sarusawa Pond. This event served as the motif for the {{ill|Uneme (Noh)|ja|采女 (謡曲)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. : As a memorial to her spirit, an annual festival – the {{ill|Uneme Festival|ja|采女祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – is held during the time of the {{ill|Mid-Autumn Moon|ja|中秋の名月|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at the {{ill|Uneme Shrine|ja|采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, located along the banks of {{ill|Sarusawa Pond|ja|猿沢池|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nara. * The Yama no I Legend *: In a legend from Koriyama City, a prelude and sequel exist: It is said that when the Katsuragi-ō (who had come on an inspection tour to Mutsu Province) first laid eyes on Haruhime, the daughter of the head of the Azumi village, he brought her back to the capital. However, missing her betrothed, Haruhime feigned an accidental plunge into Sarusawa Pond in order to return home. Later, after her lover cast himself into the clear waters of a mountain well, Haruhime followed him in a final act of suicide. In connection with this legend, the local {{ill|Uneme Shrine (Koriyama)|ja|采女神社 (郡山市)|lt=Uneme Shrine|lt_ja=采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} exists, as does a local festival – the {{ill|Koriyama Uneme Festival|ja|郡山うねめまつり|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – established at the time of the merger of Koriyama City and {{ill|Azumi District|ja|安積郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. There is also a tourism ambassador known as “Miss Uneme” who is selected through a {{ill|Miss Contest|ja|ミスコンテスト|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. === Kojiki Legend === : During the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} that “the threefold Uneme of {{ill|Ise Province|ja|伊勢の国|qq=draft|qq=draft}},” while serving at a banquet for the emperor, unwittingly poured wine into a ceremonial cup containing leaves. This act incurred the emperor’s wrath and nearly led to her execution; however, she spontaneously composed a poem extolling the emperor and praying for prosperity, and the excellence of her verse so impressed the emperor that her life was spared. Furthermore, a place named “Uneme” exists in both {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yokkaichi City|ja|四日市市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

{{ill|Imperial Harem|ja|後宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Court Lady|ja|女官|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Former Han Dynasty|ja|前漢|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Tang Dynasty|ja|唐|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Imperial Court|ja|朝廷|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Empress|ja|皇后|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Official Position|ja|官職|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
'''Uneme''' (采女)
# In China, the term Uneme has two distinct meanings: # In China, Uneme (pronounced “saijo”) refers to an official system found in dynasties following the {{ill|Former Han Dynasty|ja|前漢|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, although it is not seen in the {{ill|Tang Dynasty|ja|唐|qq=draft|qq=draft}} system.<ref name="sogabe" /> # In Japan, Uneme (pronounced “uneme”) were court ladies who served in the {{ill|Imperial Court|ja|朝廷|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, attending closely to the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Empress|ja|皇后|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by managing meals and other daily affairs – an official post which existed until the early {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in China == === Han Dynasty === In the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, accounts are found in Volume 8 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Ling|ja|霊帝 (漢)|lt=Emperor Ling|lt_ja=霊帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and in Volume 10, Part 1 of the harem annals.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to the biography of {{ill|Lu Qiang|ja|呂強|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the number of harem {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was said to number in the thousands, with the term “Uneme” being synonymous with “Cai Nu”.<ref name="sogabe" /> Although the Uneme system was not adopted under the Tang system and was regarded as a Later Han institution, the first volume of the {{ill|Miscellaneous Records of Xijing|ja|西京雑記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} contains an account of “Cai Nu”, suggesting that its origins may extend as far back as the Former Han.<ref name="sogabe" />
=== After the Han Dynasty === The {{ill|Book of Jin|ja|晋書|qq=draft|qq=draft}} discusses the Uneme of {{ill|Emperor Wu of Jin|ja|司馬炎|lt=Emperor Wu of Jin|lt_ja=武帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, with accounts appearing in Volume 3 of the annals of Emperor Wu, Volume 57 of the biography of {{ill|Hu Fen|ja|胡奮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Volume 27 of the upper Five Elements Records, Volume 28 of the middle Five Elements Records, and Volume 31 of the consorts’ records.<ref name="sogabe" />
Regarding the Southern and Northern Dynasties period, the {{ill|History of the Southern Dynasties|ja|南史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Song Dynasty (Southern)|ja|宋 (南朝)|lt=Southern Song|lt_ja=宋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records in Volume 2 that the deposed former emperor {{ill|Former Deposed Emperor|ja|前廃帝 (南朝宋)|lt=Former Deposed Emperor|lt_ja=前廃帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the {{ill|Princess of the Mountain Shade|ja|山陰公主|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and several hundred {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, followed an assembly of shamans to capture ghosts; further mentions of Uneme appear in Volume 11 in the biography of {{ill|Chen Miaodeng|ja|陳妙登|lt=Later Deposed Empress Chen|lt_ja=後廃帝陳太妃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" /> In the {{ill|Book of Northern History|ja|北史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Northern Wei|ja|北魏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (or later Wei), Volume 13 of the consorts’ records notes the existence of the Uneme system, and Volume 10 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou|ja|宣帝 (北周)|lt=Emperor Xuan|lt_ja=宣帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes an account of Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" />
During the {{ill|Sui Dynasty|ja|隋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} period, Volume 675 of the {{ill|Wenyuan Yinghua|ja|文苑英華|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that in Emperor {{ill|Yang of Sui|ja|煬帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s harem there were said to be several hundred to a thousand Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to {{ill|Zhao Yi|ja|趙翼|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Uneme also existed during the era of the {{ill|Yuan Dynasty|ja|元 (王朝)|lt=Yuan|lt_ja=元|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as recorded in Volume 30 of the {{ill|Annotated Twenty-Two Histories|ja|二十二史箚記|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in Japan == The earliest mention of Uneme appears in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe">{{Cite journal |type=Japanese book |url=https://doi.org/10.5955/jalha.1951.96 |author={{ill|Sogabe Shizuo|ja|曽我部静雄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=The Origins of Attendants, Uneme, and Female Servants |journal=Studies in Legal History |issue=1 |publisher=Legal History Society |date=1951 |pages=96–119}}</ref>
In the 2nd year of the {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (807 AD), the system of Uneme offerings was temporarily abolished, but it was revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, the position was reserved only for special ceremonies. The head official of the Uneme was known as Uneme-no-Kami.
=== History === Although many aspects of its origins remain unclear, according to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as early as the {{ill|Asuka Period|ja|飛鳥時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, local aristocrats customarily offered their daughters to the {{ill|Imperial Household|ja|皇室|lt=Imperial Family|lt_ja=天皇家|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Successive generations of Uneme were drawn from the direct families of the emperor as well as from prominent local clans. Moreover, a Taihōkan edict issued in the 17th year of the {{ill|Engi|ja|延喜|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (917 AD, as indicated by {{ill|917|ja|917|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) by which the governor of Izumo Province (<now rendered as> {{ill|Izumo Provincial Governor|ja|出雲国造|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) prohibited keeping a concubine under the title {{ill|Jingu Uneme|ja|神宮采女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, except in cases necessary for Shinto ritual, has been cited as evidence that the system emerged during the process in which the imperial family gradually absorbed and integrated local ritual functions. Some scholars have even suggested that Uneme, who were sometimes treated as equivalent to concubines in ritual practices that sometimes involved procreation, may have had their origins in associations with {{ill|Shrine Maidens|ja|巫女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>『古代豪族』, Aoki Kazuo</ref>
Although their principal duty was to serve in the meal preparations for the emperor, Uneme – who were exclusively selected from among those admired for their beauty from all over the country and who served in close proximity to the emperor – often also fulfilled the role of concubines and bore children. However, as social status at that time placed great importance on the mother’s family background, children born to Uneme from local aristocratic families (the families of {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and above) were generally accorded a lower status compared with those born to central aristocrats or the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The system was formalized by the Imperial Harem Officials Order of the {{ill|Taibō Ritsuryō|ja|大宝律令|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Its provisions were as follows: : An edict issued by the {{ill|Ministry of Central Affairs|ja|中務省|1=Ministry of the Center|qq=draft|qq=draft}} allocated quotas to the provinces for recruitment, though the process was nominally termed an “offering.” : The eligibility criteria were: # The candidate had to be between 13 and 30 years old. (In the revived system during {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s reign – after the temporary abolition of the offering system – the age requirement was 16 to 20.) # The candidate had to be a daughter or sister of a family of at least {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} Rank. # Their appearance had to be especially refined. : Although the personnel matters of these women were managed by the “Uneme Department” ({{ill|Uneme Department|ja|采女司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) under the {{ill|Imperial Household Ministry|ja|宮内省 (律令制)|lt=Imperial Household Ministry|lt_ja=宮内省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in practice they were assigned to two of the Twelve Harem Departments: 6 to the {{ill|Water Department|ja|水司|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 60 to the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Although the official quota was 66, the military defense provisions of the Taibō Ritsuryō stipulated that Uneme should be recruited from one-third of the provinces nationwide; thus, the actual number of Uneme offered greatly exceeded the official quota. It is therefore believed that there were also individuals placed in other departments as substitutes for {{ill|Onamutsu|ja|女嬬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or who were employed outside the official quota,<ref>『郡司及び采女制度の研究』, Isokai Masayoshi</ref> or even those attached to imperial princes,<ref>『奈良の都』, Aoki Kazuo</ref> and that some, such as {{ill|Iitakushotaka|ja|飯高諸高|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were later promoted to higher positions (such as {{ill|Dianshi|ja|典侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Chief Attendant|ja|掌侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Head of the Serving Department|ja|掌膳|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Official Sweeper|ja|典掃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), which were also considered outside the official Uneme quota. In this period when Uneme were integrated into the {{ill|Ritsuryō System|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, their role as wives or concubines of the emperor diminished, and they increasingly came to be regarded as lower-Ranking officials within the imperial harem. Many of them likely became {{ill|Maid|ja|女孺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite book |author={{ill|Keiji Nagahara|ja|永原慶二|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=Iwanami Dictionary of Japanese History |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |date=1999}}</ref>
Reforms under {{ill|Emperor Heizei|ja|平城天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} abolished the system of Uneme offerings, and accordingly the Uneme Department was also dissolved, being merged with the Department of Sewing ({{ill|Department of Sewing|ja|縫部司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in the {{ill|Sewing Hall|ja|縫殿寮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Ministry of Finance|ja|大蔵省 (律令制)|1=Ministry of the Treasury|lt=Finance Ministry|lt_ja=大蔵省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. However, the offering system and the Uneme Department were revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|Engishiki|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the official quota for Uneme was reduced to 41 in the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 6 in the {{ill|Cleaning Department|ja|掃司|lt=Kanomori no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かにもりのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, Uneme were increasingly selected from the daughters of central nobles, and the role became increasingly ceremonial. From the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} onward, Uneme were chosen from among the court ladies only at the time of the {{ill|Enthronement Ceremony|ja|即位の礼|lt=Enthronement Ceremony|lt_ja=即位式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} for the emperor; at that time, instead of wearing the full formal attire of the court ladies ({{ill|Junihitoe|ja|十二単|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), they donned a special, short {{ill|Uneme Costume|ja|采女装束|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Etymology === Several theories have been proposed regarding the origin of the word “uneme.” These include {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|ja|本居宣長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unagee” theory (嬰部（うなげえ）), {{ill|Ogyū Sorai|ja|荻生徂徠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unawime” theory (項意（うなゐめ）), {{ill|Kamo no Maifuchi|ja|賀茂真淵|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unome” theory (氏之女（うのめ）), and {{ill|Tsuboi Yoshitomo|ja|壺井義知|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Uneme” theory (畝女（うねめ）).
=== Uneme as Objects of Admiration === Uneme were reputed to be largely drawn from local aristocratic families, celebrated for their exquisite beauty and high cultural accomplishments. Owing to the fact that only the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was permitted personal contact with them, they have long been objects of male admiration. In earlier times, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} describes the Uneme as having “exceptionally beautiful features and a refined appearance,” while the {{ill|Hyakuryō Kun'yōshū|ja|百寮訓要集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} states that “the Uneme are women selected from among the most beautiful in the land to serve the Son of Heaven.” The {{ill|Kokinshū|ja|古今集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also contains many gentle allusions in its poetry, and the {{ill|Wakan Kanjō Hisho|ja|和漢官職秘抄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that “in some accounts, either through the fame of a beauty or the renown of her poetry – or by virtue of a refined aptitude in playing the koto and the se – a woman would be presented by local officials.” Furthermore, the {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes the famous poem celebrating how {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|ja|藤原鎌足|qq=draft|qq=draft}} rejoiced at receiving the Uneme Yasumi from {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: “われはもや安見児得たり 皆人の得難にすとふ安見児得たり” In addition, a poem by {{ill|Prince Shiki|ja|志貴皇子|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—“The Uneme’s sleeves flutter, like the Asuka breeze, playfully blowing far from the capital”—reveals the deep admiration that men felt for these beautiful Uneme.
== Legendary Uneme == === The Legend of Sarusawa Pond / Yama no I Legend === : In the {{ill|Yamato Monogatari|ja|大和物語|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, there is a legend concerning the “Emperor of Nara” (displayed as {{ill|Tachibana Morone|ja|橘諸兄|lt=Katsuragi-ō|lt_ja=葛城王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and an Uneme known as Haruhime. : It is noteworthy that interpretations of the related Man'yōshū poems differ between the two versions—for instance, whether the poem “Even the shadows of Mount Azumi can be seen in the shallow heart of the mountain well” conveys a sentiment of passionate love or sincere devotion, and whether the poem “My sister’s disheveled hair, I see it sorrowfully in the jeweled waters of Sarusawa Pond” evokes the image of hair floating like seaweed from a drowned body or recalls the hair as it was in life. : On the basis of this legend, {{ill|Nara City|ja|奈良市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Koriyama City|ja|郡山市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} have established a sister cities relationship. * Sarusawa Pond *: According to both the account in the Yamato Monogatari and local tradition in Nara City, a certain Uneme—who had fallen out of favor with the “Emperor of Nara” (during the {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, referred to as Saru Tennō)—committed suicide by leaping into Sarusawa Pond. This event served as the motif for the {{ill|Uneme (Noh)|ja|采女 (謡曲)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. : As a memorial to her spirit, an annual festival – the {{ill|Uneme Festival|ja|采女祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – is held during the time of the {{ill|Mid-Autumn Moon|ja|中秋の名月|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at the {{ill|Uneme Shrine|ja|采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, located along the banks of {{ill|Sarusawa Pond|ja|猿沢池|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nara. * The Yama no I Legend *: In a legend from Koriyama City, a prelude and sequel exist: It is said that when the Katsuragi-ō (who had come on an inspection tour to Mutsu Province) first laid eyes on Haruhime, the daughter of the head of the Azumi village, he brought her back to the capital. However, missing her betrothed, Haruhime feigned an accidental plunge into Sarusawa Pond in order to return home. Later, after her lover cast himself into the clear waters of a mountain well, Haruhime followed him in a final act of suicide. In connection with this legend, the local {{ill|Uneme Shrine (Koriyama)|ja|采女神社 (郡山市)|lt=Uneme Shrine|lt_ja=采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} exists, as does a local festival – the {{ill|Koriyama Uneme Festival|ja|郡山うねめまつり|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – established at the time of the merger of Koriyama City and {{ill|Azumi District|ja|安積郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. There is also a tourism ambassador known as “Miss Uneme” who is selected through a {{ill|Miss Contest|ja|ミスコンテスト|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. === Kojiki Legend === : During the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} that “the threefold Uneme of {{ill|Ise Province|ja|伊勢の国|qq=draft|qq=draft}},” while serving at a banquet for the emperor, unwittingly poured wine into a ceremonial cup containing leaves. This act incurred the emperor’s wrath and nearly led to her execution; however, she spontaneously composed a poem extolling the emperor and praying for prosperity, and the excellence of her verse so impressed the emperor that her life was spared. Furthermore, a place named “Uneme” exists in both {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yokkaichi City|ja|四日市市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

{{ill|Imperial Harem|ja|後宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Court Lady|ja|女官|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Former Han Dynasty|ja|前漢|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Tang Dynasty|ja|唐|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Imperial Court|ja|朝廷|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Empress|ja|皇后|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{ill|Official Position|ja|官職|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
'''Uneme''' (采女)
# In China, the term Uneme has two distinct meanings: # In China, Uneme (pronounced “saijo”) refers to an official system found in dynasties following the {{ill|Former Han Dynasty|ja|前漢|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, although it is not seen in the {{ill|Tang Dynasty|ja|唐|qq=draft|qq=draft}} system.<ref name="sogabe" /> # In Japan, Uneme (pronounced “uneme”) were court ladies who served in the {{ill|Imperial Court|ja|朝廷|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, attending closely to the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Empress|ja|皇后|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by managing meals and other daily affairs – an official post which existed until the early {{ill|Heian Period|ja|平安時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in China == === Han Dynasty === In the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, accounts are found in Volume 8 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Ling|ja|霊帝 (漢)|lt=Emperor Ling|lt_ja=霊帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and in Volume 10, Part 1 of the harem annals.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to the biography of {{ill|Lu Qiang|ja|呂強|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the {{ill|Book of the Later Han|ja|後漢書|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the number of harem {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was said to number in the thousands, with the term “Uneme” being synonymous with “Cai Nu”.<ref name="sogabe" /> Although the Uneme system was not adopted under the Tang system and was regarded as a Later Han institution, the first volume of the {{ill|Miscellaneous Records of Xijing|ja|西京雑記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} contains an account of “Cai Nu”, suggesting that its origins may extend as far back as the Former Han.<ref name="sogabe" />
=== After the Han Dynasty === The {{ill|Book of Jin|ja|晋書|qq=draft|qq=draft}} discusses the Uneme of {{ill|Emperor Wu of Jin|ja|司馬炎|lt=Emperor Wu of Jin|lt_ja=武帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, with accounts appearing in Volume 3 of the annals of Emperor Wu, Volume 57 of the biography of {{ill|Hu Fen|ja|胡奮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Volume 27 of the upper Five Elements Records, Volume 28 of the middle Five Elements Records, and Volume 31 of the consorts’ records.<ref name="sogabe" />
Regarding the Southern and Northern Dynasties period, the {{ill|History of the Southern Dynasties|ja|南史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Song Dynasty (Southern)|ja|宋 (南朝)|lt=Southern Song|lt_ja=宋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records in Volume 2 that the deposed former emperor {{ill|Former Deposed Emperor|ja|前廃帝 (南朝宋)|lt=Former Deposed Emperor|lt_ja=前廃帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the {{ill|Princess of the Mountain Shade|ja|山陰公主|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and several hundred {{ill|Cai Nu|ja|綵女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, followed an assembly of shamans to capture ghosts; further mentions of Uneme appear in Volume 11 in the biography of {{ill|Chen Miaodeng|ja|陳妙登|lt=Later Deposed Empress Chen|lt_ja=後廃帝陳太妃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" /> In the {{ill|Book of Northern History|ja|北史|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Northern Wei|ja|北魏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (or later Wei), Volume 13 of the consorts’ records notes the existence of the Uneme system, and Volume 10 of the annals of {{ill|Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou|ja|宣帝 (北周)|lt=Emperor Xuan|lt_ja=宣帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes an account of Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" />
During the {{ill|Sui Dynasty|ja|隋|qq=draft|qq=draft}} period, Volume 675 of the {{ill|Wenyuan Yinghua|ja|文苑英華|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that in Emperor {{ill|Yang of Sui|ja|煬帝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s harem there were said to be several hundred to a thousand Uneme.<ref name="sogabe" /> According to {{ill|Zhao Yi|ja|趙翼|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Uneme also existed during the era of the {{ill|Yuan Dynasty|ja|元 (王朝)|lt=Yuan|lt_ja=元|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as recorded in Volume 30 of the {{ill|Annotated Twenty-Two Histories|ja|二十二史箚記|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe" />
== Uneme in Japan == The earliest mention of Uneme appears in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the section on {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref name="sogabe">{{Cite journal |type=Japanese book |url=https://doi.org/10.5955/jalha.1951.96 |author={{ill|Sogabe Shizuo|ja|曽我部静雄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=The Origins of Attendants, Uneme, and Female Servants |journal=Studies in Legal History |issue=1 |publisher=Legal History Society |date=1951 |pages=96–119}}</ref>
In the 2nd year of the {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)|lt=Daidō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (807 AD), the system of Uneme offerings was temporarily abolished, but it was revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, the position was reserved only for special ceremonies. The head official of the Uneme was known as Uneme-no-Kami.
=== History === Although many aspects of its origins remain unclear, according to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as early as the {{ill|Asuka Period|ja|飛鳥時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, local aristocrats customarily offered their daughters to the {{ill|Imperial Household|ja|皇室|lt=Imperial Family|lt_ja=天皇家|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Successive generations of Uneme were drawn from the direct families of the emperor as well as from prominent local clans. Moreover, a Taihōkan edict issued in the 17th year of the {{ill|Engi|ja|延喜|qq=draft|qq=draft}} era (917 AD, as indicated by {{ill|917|ja|917|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) by which the governor of Izumo Province (<now rendered as> {{ill|Izumo Provincial Governor|ja|出雲国造|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) prohibited keeping a concubine under the title {{ill|Jingu Uneme|ja|神宮采女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, except in cases necessary for Shinto ritual, has been cited as evidence that the system emerged during the process in which the imperial family gradually absorbed and integrated local ritual functions. Some scholars have even suggested that Uneme, who were sometimes treated as equivalent to concubines in ritual practices that sometimes involved procreation, may have had their origins in associations with {{ill|Shrine Maidens|ja|巫女|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>『古代豪族』, Aoki Kazuo</ref>
Although their principal duty was to serve in the meal preparations for the emperor, Uneme – who were exclusively selected from among those admired for their beauty from all over the country and who served in close proximity to the emperor – often also fulfilled the role of concubines and bore children. However, as social status at that time placed great importance on the mother’s family background, children born to Uneme from local aristocratic families (the families of {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and above) were generally accorded a lower status compared with those born to central aristocrats or the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The system was formalized by the Imperial Harem Officials Order of the {{ill|Taibō Ritsuryō|ja|大宝律令|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Its provisions were as follows: : An edict issued by the {{ill|Ministry of Central Affairs|ja|中務省|1=Ministry of the Center|qq=draft|qq=draft}} allocated quotas to the provinces for recruitment, though the process was nominally termed an “offering.” : The eligibility criteria were: # The candidate had to be between 13 and 30 years old. (In the revived system during {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s reign – after the temporary abolition of the offering system – the age requirement was 16 to 20.) # The candidate had to be a daughter or sister of a family of at least {{ill|County Magistrate|ja|郡司|lt=Deputy County Magistrate|lt_ja=郡少領|qq=draft|qq=draft}} Rank. # Their appearance had to be especially refined. : Although the personnel matters of these women were managed by the “Uneme Department” ({{ill|Uneme Department|ja|采女司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) under the {{ill|Imperial Household Ministry|ja|宮内省 (律令制)|lt=Imperial Household Ministry|lt_ja=宮内省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in practice they were assigned to two of the Twelve Harem Departments: 6 to the {{ill|Water Department|ja|水司|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 60 to the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Although the official quota was 66, the military defense provisions of the Taibō Ritsuryō stipulated that Uneme should be recruited from one-third of the provinces nationwide; thus, the actual number of Uneme offered greatly exceeded the official quota. It is therefore believed that there were also individuals placed in other departments as substitutes for {{ill|Onamutsu|ja|女嬬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or who were employed outside the official quota,<ref>『郡司及び采女制度の研究』, Isokai Masayoshi</ref> or even those attached to imperial princes,<ref>『奈良の都』, Aoki Kazuo</ref> and that some, such as {{ill|Iitakushotaka|ja|飯高諸高|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were later promoted to higher positions (such as {{ill|Dianshi|ja|典侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Chief Attendant|ja|掌侍|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Head of the Serving Department|ja|掌膳|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, or {{ill|Official Sweeper|ja|典掃|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), which were also considered outside the official Uneme quota. In this period when Uneme were integrated into the {{ill|Ritsuryō System|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, their role as wives or concubines of the emperor diminished, and they increasingly came to be regarded as lower-Ranking officials within the imperial harem. Many of them likely became {{ill|Maid|ja|女孺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>{{Cite book |author={{ill|Keiji Nagahara|ja|永原慶二|qq=draft|qq=draft}} |title=Iwanami Dictionary of Japanese History |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |date=1999}}</ref>
Reforms under {{ill|Emperor Heizei|ja|平城天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} abolished the system of Uneme offerings, and accordingly the Uneme Department was also dissolved, being merged with the Department of Sewing ({{ill|Department of Sewing|ja|縫部司|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in the {{ill|Sewing Hall|ja|縫殿寮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the {{ill|Ministry of Finance|ja|大蔵省 (律令制)|1=Ministry of the Treasury|lt=Finance Ministry|lt_ja=大蔵省|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. However, the offering system and the Uneme Department were revived during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Saga|ja|嵯峨天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|Engishiki|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the official quota for Uneme was reduced to 41 in the {{ill|Serving Department|ja|膳司|lt=Kashiwade no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かしわでのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and 6 in the {{ill|Cleaning Department|ja|掃司|lt=Kanomori no Tsukasa|lt_ja=かにもりのつかさ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Thereafter, Uneme were increasingly selected from the daughters of central nobles, and the role became increasingly ceremonial. From the {{ill|Edo Period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} onward, Uneme were chosen from among the court ladies only at the time of the {{ill|Enthronement Ceremony|ja|即位の礼|lt=Enthronement Ceremony|lt_ja=即位式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} for the emperor; at that time, instead of wearing the full formal attire of the court ladies ({{ill|Junihitoe|ja|十二単|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), they donned a special, short {{ill|Uneme Costume|ja|采女装束|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Etymology === Several theories have been proposed regarding the origin of the word “uneme.” These include {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|ja|本居宣長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unagee” theory (嬰部（うなげえ）), {{ill|Ogyū Sorai|ja|荻生徂徠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unawime” theory (項意（うなゐめ）), {{ill|Kamo no Maifuchi|ja|賀茂真淵|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Unome” theory (氏之女（うのめ）), and {{ill|Tsuboi Yoshitomo|ja|壺井義知|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s “Uneme” theory (畝女（うねめ）).
=== Uneme as Objects of Admiration === Uneme were reputed to be largely drawn from local aristocratic families, celebrated for their exquisite beauty and high cultural accomplishments. Owing to the fact that only the {{ill|Emperor|ja|天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was permitted personal contact with them, they have long been objects of male admiration. In earlier times, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s section on {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}} describes the Uneme as having “exceptionally beautiful features and a refined appearance,” while the {{ill|Hyakuryō Kun'yōshū|ja|百寮訓要集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} states that “the Uneme are women selected from among the most beautiful in the land to serve the Son of Heaven.” The {{ill|Kokinshū|ja|古今集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also contains many gentle allusions in its poetry, and the {{ill|Wakan Kanjō Hisho|ja|和漢官職秘抄|qq=draft|qq=draft}} records that “in some accounts, either through the fame of a beauty or the renown of her poetry – or by virtue of a refined aptitude in playing the koto and the se – a woman would be presented by local officials.” Furthermore, the {{ill|Man'yōshū|ja|万葉集|qq=draft|qq=draft}} includes the famous poem celebrating how {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|ja|藤原鎌足|qq=draft|qq=draft}} rejoiced at receiving the Uneme Yasumi from {{ill|Emperor Tenji|ja|天智天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: “われはもや安見児得たり 皆人の得難にすとふ安見児得たり” In addition, a poem by {{ill|Prince Shiki|ja|志貴皇子|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—“The Uneme’s sleeves flutter, like the Asuka breeze, playfully blowing far from the capital”—reveals the deep admiration that men felt for these beautiful Uneme.
== Legendary Uneme == === The Legend of Sarusawa Pond / Yama no I Legend === : In the {{ill|Yamato Monogatari|ja|大和物語|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, there is a legend concerning the “Emperor of Nara” (displayed as {{ill|Tachibana Morone|ja|橘諸兄|lt=Katsuragi-ō|lt_ja=葛城王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and an Uneme known as Haruhime. : It is noteworthy that interpretations of the related Man'yōshū poems differ between the two versions—for instance, whether the poem “Even the shadows of Mount Azumi can be seen in the shallow heart of the mountain well” conveys a sentiment of passionate love or sincere devotion, and whether the poem “My sister’s disheveled hair, I see it sorrowfully in the jeweled waters of Sarusawa Pond” evokes the image of hair floating like seaweed from a drowned body or recalls the hair as it was in life. : On the basis of this legend, {{ill|Nara City|ja|奈良市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Koriyama City|ja|郡山市|qq=draft|qq=draft}} have established a sister cities relationship. * Sarusawa Pond *: According to both the account in the Yamato Monogatari and local tradition in Nara City, a certain Uneme—who had fallen out of favor with the “Emperor of Nara” (during the {{ill|Nara Period|ja|奈良時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, referred to as Saru Tennō)—committed suicide by leaping into Sarusawa Pond. This event served as the motif for the {{ill|Uneme (Noh)|ja|采女 (謡曲)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. : As a memorial to her spirit, an annual festival – the {{ill|Uneme Festival|ja|采女祭|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – is held during the time of the {{ill|Mid-Autumn Moon|ja|中秋の名月|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at the {{ill|Uneme Shrine|ja|采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, located along the banks of {{ill|Sarusawa Pond|ja|猿沢池|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nara. * The Yama no I Legend *: In a legend from Koriyama City, a prelude and sequel exist: It is said that when the Katsuragi-ō (who had come on an inspection tour to Mutsu Province) first laid eyes on Haruhime, the daughter of the head of the Azumi village, he brought her back to the capital. However, missing her betrothed, Haruhime feigned an accidental plunge into Sarusawa Pond in order to return home. Later, after her lover cast himself into the clear waters of a mountain well, Haruhime followed him in a final act of suicide. In connection with this legend, the local {{ill|Uneme Shrine (Koriyama)|ja|采女神社 (郡山市)|lt=Uneme Shrine|lt_ja=采女神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} exists, as does a local festival – the {{ill|Koriyama Uneme Festival|ja|郡山うねめまつり|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – established at the time of the merger of Koriyama City and {{ill|Azumi District|ja|安積郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. There is also a tourism ambassador known as “Miss Uneme” who is selected through a {{ill|Miss Contest|ja|ミスコンテスト|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. === Kojiki Legend === : During the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yuryaku|ja|雄略天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is recorded in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|qq=draft|qq=draft}} that “the threefold Uneme of {{ill|Ise Province|ja|伊勢の国|qq=draft|qq=draft}},” while serving at a banquet for the emperor, unwittingly poured wine into a ceremonial cup containing leaves. This act incurred the emperor’s wrath and nearly led to her execution; however, she spontaneously composed a poem extolling the emperor and praying for prosperity, and the excellence of her verse so impressed the emperor that her life was spared. Furthermore, a place named “Uneme” exists in both {{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yokkaichi City|ja|四日市市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
